question_text: A 23-year-old man comes to the physician for frequent and painful urination. He has also had progressive painful swelling of his right knee over the past week. He is sexually active with two female partners and uses condoms inconsistently. His mother has an autoimmune disease that involves a malar rash. Examination shows conjunctivitis bilaterally. The right knee is warm, erythematous, and tender to touch; range of motion is limited. Laboratory studies show an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 62 mm/h. Urinalysis shows WBCs. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to reveal which of the following?

                    ### Question
                    A 23-year-old man comes to the physician for frequent and painful urination. He has also had progressive painful swelling of his right knee over the past week. He is sexually active with two female partners and uses condoms inconsistently. His mother has an autoimmune disease that involves a malar rash. Examination shows conjunctivitis bilaterally. The right knee is warm, erythematous, and tender to touch; range of motion is limited. Laboratory studies show an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 62 mm/h. Urinalysis shows WBCs. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to reveal which of the following?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Hiking trip two months ago
opb. Recent norovirus gastroenteritis
opc. Positive anti-dsDNA antibodies
opd. Chondrocalcinosis of the left knee
ope. HLA-B27 positive genotype

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The 23-year-old man's symptoms of frequent painful urination and progressive swelling of the right knee, along with bilateral conjunctivitis and a family history of autoimmune disease, suggest a systemic inflammatory condition. The elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate indicates significant inflammation. The presence of conjunctivitis and joint symptoms, combined with the family history, raises suspicion for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), which is characterized by positive anti-dsDNA antibodies. While reactive arthritis due to a sexually transmitted infection is a possibility, the strong association of anti-dsDNA antibodies with lupus, especially given the family history, makes it the most likely finding. Therefore, the most relevant and consensus-supported conclusion is that further evaluation is likely to reveal positive anti-dsDNA antibodies.
